profile.summary: The Jores et al. 2021 study measured the strength of tens of thousands of Arabidopsis, maize and sorghum core promoters with a STARR-seq reporter assay in tobacco leaves and maize protoplasts, then trained a linear model and a convolutional neural network to predict promoter strength from sequence, scored on a random 10% hold-out. It is a reference point for plant regulatory sequence models, for example when comparing a DNA model's promoter strength predictions in the two assay systems.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well a model predicts core promoter strength, the log2 enrichment of a promoter's reporter output relative to the 35S minimal promoter, from the promoter DNA sequence. There are two tasks, one per assay system: transiently transformed tobacco leaves (a dicot) and maize protoplasts (a monocot).

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Three STARR-seq libraries held 18,329 Arabidopsis, 34,415 maize and 27,094 sorghum core promoters, each also built with an upstream 35S enhancer. Models use the libraries with the enhancer, measured in the dark. In modelling.R the split is random: within each assay system and species, each promoter is assigned to train or test with probability 0.9 and 0.1 (seed 1).

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Predictions on the held-out 10% are compared with measured strength by Pearson R2 (and Spearman correlation in the repository's stats files), overall and per species. The linear model (GC content plus maximum motif scores for six core promoter elements and 72 TF motifs) explained 51% (tobacco) and 45% (maize) of variance; the CNN reached R2 0.71 and 0.67.

notes: The test files CNN/CNN_test_leaf.tsv and CNN/CNN_test_proto.tsv have 7155 and 7596 lines including a header (counted by Rewire), that is 7154 and 7595 promoters; no source prints these counts, so the structured sizes are null. modelling.R writes the CNN train and test files from its own split in code that is now commented out, which suggests, but does not prove, that the linear and CNN models share one split. The published article may be paywalled; the copy used is the PDF on the Queitsch lab site named in the record's existing source. The repository has no licence (GitHub API licence: null), so all files are marked not for redistribution.
